description:
We are Space Valley (team Halal Haemek) from Haifa: Daniel Turgeman and Maor Buzaglo. We love space, data and building things people can play with. For NASA Space Apps 2026 we built SPHEREx Blink, a web and VR tool that lets anyone hunt for Planet X, brown dwarfs, comets and exo-planets in NASA's SPHEREx images. 
Try our tool here: https://spherex-blink.github.io/
summary: SPHEREx Blink (https://spherex-blink.github.io) lets anyone hunt for Planet X, hidden brown dwarfs and new comets in NASA's newest infrared sky survey, right in the browser. NASA's SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, and its archive already holds 1.6 million images. Objects that move or change only reveal themselves when images from different times are compared, but there was no public tool to blink SPHEREx images. Click any point of the sky and within about two seconds you see a video of that spot across every SPHEREx visit, aligned to 0.01 pixel and read straight from NASA's archive with no server, so new data appears automatically. Built-in discovery tools take you from a click to a candidate: a difference view, a detection filter, motion measurement, shift-and-stack deep stacks for movers too faint for single images, light curves and spectra, asteroid and comet positions, and shareable links. It also runs on a sky dome and in any VR headset. On NASA's test targets the tools reproduce Barnard's Star's motion (96% of the catalogue value), reveal the brown dwarf WISE 0855, and recover R Draconis's 239-day cycle. With Canada's NEOSSat data we show the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS crossing the stars in one hour, together with SPHEREx.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx Blink (https://spherex-blink.github.io) turns NASA's SPHEREx archive into a discovery tool anyone can use. Pick any point on an all-sky SPHEREx map, or type a name or coordinates, and within about two seconds you see a short video of that spot across every SPHEREx visit. Cold worlds such as a possible Planet X or a nearby brown dwarf, asteroids and comets give themselves away by moving between visits, and variable stars by changing brightness.

HOW IT WORKS

- No server, always current: we built an index of all 1.63 million SPHEREx images (results identical to NASA's own IRSA search, in 15-200 ms instead of up to ~100 s). The browser reads only the pixels it needs straight from NASA's public archive, and the index refreshes daily, so new data releases appear automatically.

- Honest pixels: every frame is aligned to 0.01 pixel using each image's full distortion model; each frame shows its detector and wavelength; exposures are stacked per visit to remove cosmic rays; saturated cores are shown as "no data", never hidden.

- Built-in discovery tools, from a click to a candidate: difference view (red = now, blue = before); a detection filter that flags sources above a chosen threshold, or only what changed; motion measurement from the pixels; shift-and-stack deep stacks that reveal movers too faint for any single image; light curves and spectra on the fly from the 102 colours; an asteroid and comet mode with positions computed as seen from SPHEREx (JPL Horizons); saved points and shareable links with coordinates in the URL.

- Three ways to look: a 2D view, a sky dome, and a VR mode for any WebXR headset.

RESULTS (VALIDITY)

All measured from raw NASA data on the challenge's test targets: Barnard's Star's motion reproduced to 96% of the catalogue value; the brown dwarf WISE 0855, invisible in every single image, detected by stacking 45 exposures (S/N ~11); R Draconis's pulsation period measured as 239 days (published ~245) although it saturates the detector; RW Aurigae 40% fainter at 4-5 µm within a year; Epsilon Indi B steady as expected. Our brightness measurements agree with NASA's WISE catalogue to about 3%.

CANADIAN SPACE AGENCY DATA

We combined Canada's NEOSSat space telescope with SPHEREx. NEOSSat took 3,699 images of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, one every 1.7 minutes, so in our tool you watch the comet cross the stars in one hour, something SPHEREx's slower revisits cannot show. On one timeline we show the comet in visible light (NEOSSat) and infrared (SPHEREx), predict its position to 1.2 arcseconds using NEOSSat's own orbit, and measure it brightening 86x near the Sun. Of 277 asteroids and comets we searched, 30 were imaged by both telescopes.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Blinking images is how volunteers found new brown dwarfs in older surveys. SPHEREx Blink makes the same thing possible for NASA's newest survey, for students, amateurs and citizen scientists, with no installation, no account and no cost. Detections are clearly labelled as candidates until confirmed.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a static image viewer, we built a living sky you can fly through: the zoom cone keeps the context of where you are, nearby tiles load around your pick, and the VR mode lets you stand inside the infrared sky and point at what moves. Combining two space agencies' telescopes on one timeline shows the same comet in two kinds of light.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy) for the data pipeline and validation; a dependency-free JavaScript data layer in the browser, tested against the Python reference; three.js and WebXR for the sky dome and VR; hosted free on GitHub Pages. Tested on desktop browsers and a Meta Quest 3 headset. Open source under the MIT license.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (alignment, wavelength labels, saturation shown, candidates not discoveries), speed (a video in seconds), staying current with weekly data releases without a server to maintain, accessibility for non-experts (a guided walkthrough), and high proper-motion targets, whose positions we propagate to each observation epoch.
